newsitem.title: UK: Gold's fall eclipses other commodity action.
newsitem.headline: Gold's fall eclipses other commodity action.

text.p: The price of gold fell to its lowest in three years on Tuesday. Wheat prices also eased but crude oil held most of the gains from a brisk new rally staged late on Monday.
Gold was the Cinderella of the commodity complex, tumbling to a London fixing of $367.40 an ounce, lowest since November 1993, after speculators abandoned it.

It closed London at $367.85 then slipped again, just below $366.50. Bullion is down from $418 in February and broke under psychological support at $370 an ounce overnight, pressured by the strong dollar.
Dealers and analysts said mining houses, particularly in Australia, have been in a panic to sell their output forward and lock in prices as the gold price sinks.
Persistent market talk that a central bank has been selling some of its gold reserves has also helped depress the mood.
"In the short term, (gold) prices will slowly erode away, and rallies will be increasingly sold into. We're definitely heading south," said metals analyst Ted Arnold of Merrill Lynch.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see gold back at $330 in 1997."
Crude oil was firm after a late rally on Monday, trading in London's Tuesday afternoon just above $23.50 per barrel.
Bad weather had closed loading ports in Mexico, even as strong fundamental gasoline and heating oil demand was seen in the United States.
Copper prices were little changed around lower levels to which they fell on Monday on a belief that a draw on stocks that fuelled a recent rally may be ending.
Last afternoon kerb business on the London Metal Exchange (LME) was at $2,183 per tonne compared with $2,187 on Monday and a 6-month peak of $2,313 last week.

LME warehouse stocks were reported up just 1,000 tonnes in latest data available on Tuesday, after a build of up to 4,000 tonnes had been expected. But the market remains critically short of metal, traders add, and was volatile through the day.
"It is stuck in a $50 range, but the option declaration is keeping the market on edge." said Martin Squires analyst at brokers Rudolf Wolff and Co.

He was referring to Wednesday's LME December options declarations which was a big factor behind recent volatility as various strike prices, from $2,300 to $2,600 swung in and out of play, prompting bouts of covering and liquidation.
Chicago Board of Trade wheat futures were lower in early Tuesday activity on news of the posting of delivery notices totalling 700,000 bushels on the December contract, traders said.
An increase in an estimate for the Australian wheat crop also weighed on the market, they said.
The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics raised its forecast for the country's 1996-97 wheat crop to 21.3 million tonnes from the previous forecast for 20.9 million.

December was down almost eight cents ar around $3.85 per bushel towards mid-session. Coffee was steadier after a fall last week and cocoa firmed to end in London at 944 pounds sterling a tonne on the March contract, up 23 sterling from Monday.
British cocoa analysts PCR Ltd estimated a world cocoa supply deficit in 1996/97 (October-September) at 127,000 tonnes compared with a surplus of 186,000 tonnes seen in 1995/96.
A stocks/consumption ratio at 39 percent, lowest for 10 years, could be a pointer to prices heading higher.

Selling that began in New York hit sugar futures. The London white sugar contract slumped to psychological support at $300 per tonne. Commission house and broker selling accounted for the bulk of the decline.
